title: Two-dimensional crystals catalyse hydrogen into protons

paper_content.abstract:
Two-dimensional (2D) crystals with atomic-level thickness dramatically shortens the
gas transport pathways, rendering it exceptionally promising for separation membrane
applications. While defect-free 2D crystals such as graphene have long been considered
impermeable to all gases, recent studies show that pristine monolayer graphene permits
room-temperature hydrogen permeation. However, the identity of the permeating species
and its generalizability to other 2D materials remain unclear. Herein, we report hydrogen
permeation behaviour through varying 2D crystals at elevated temperature, and the
hydrogen permeability of graphene can reach up to 1017 s-1m-2 as the form of protons.
This process is evidenced by three critical steps: 2D crystals-assisted catalytic
dissociation of hydrogen into protons, protons permeation through the 2D crystals lattice,
and proton recombination after permeation. Interestingly, the activation energy remains
invariant with the layer number of 2D crystals, but the permeability and activation energy
can be modulated by the type of materials, adsorbed metal nanoparticles, and the
external atmosphere. These findings reveal a catalysis-driven proton permeation
mechanism, and fundamentally deepen the understanding of hydrogen permeation
through 2D crystals.
paper_content.introduction:
High-performance membranes with exceptional permeability, selectivity and stability are the
cornerstone of membrane separation technology1. Graphene and other two-dimensional (2D)
crystals, featuring atomic-scale thickness, can minimize gas transport pathways and significantly
reduce energy consumption, making them highly promising candidates for next-generation
separation membranes2. Nevertheless, it has been conventionally established that defect-free
graphene exhibits complete impermeability to all gas molecules, attributable to its densely packed
hexagonal lattice and delocalized π-electron cloud3-5. Conventional strategies focus on the
deliberate defect engineering through chemical or structural modifications that disrupt the inherent
atomic arrangement of graphene2,6-12. This leads to uneven pore size while also compromising the
stability and lifespan of graphene1.

Pristine graphene, with its atomically perfect sp2-hybridized hexagonal lattice, uniform pore
distribution, and sub-angstrom structural regularity, represents an ideal framework for molecular
sieving. Emerging experimental studies have begun to explore the separation properties of such
defect-free graphene. Recent work has demonstrated a room temperature (RT) cooperative
catalytic dissociation-permeation process of hydrogen molecules (H ) on defect-free monolayer
2
(1L) graphene13. This finding offers new insights for the development of graphene-based
permeation membranes. A key prerequisite for this process is the catalytic dissociation of H on
2
the surface of graphene, which is traditionally regarded as chemically inert13,14. Building on this
initial report of RT H permeation13, a deeper understanding of the inherent catalytic-permeation
2
properties of defect-free graphene and related 2D crystals is essential. Nevertheless, several critical
issues remain, including: (1) the catalytic-permeation stability of graphene at the elevated
temperatures; (2) the specific species of H dissociation; (3) the influence of material layer number;
2
(4) strategies to regulate the permeation barrier; (5) the universality of 2D crystals. Resolving these
aspects is essential for a deeper mechanistic understanding and for generalizing the observed
behaviour, with potential implications for applications such as high‑temperature
proton‑conducting fuel cells and catalytic membrane reactors in hydrogen‑based processes15-17.
Therefore, it is urgent to systematically investigate the catalytic and permeation properties of
pristine graphene and related 2D crystals.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, the authors demonstrate an intriguing behavior of hydrogen gas permeation through defect-free atomically-thin membranes. Although the report is more phenomenologically, I believe there is fundamentally important mechanisms underneath. Therefore, I highly recommend its publication to the community that may attract more attentions and promote the discovery of new physics.
To my knowledge, catalytic dissociation of hydrogen gas via 2D surfaces at relatively high temperatures (here, up to 900 °C) was not reported previously. More importantly, at this temperature, whether and how proton permeates through multilayer 2D materials remain an interesting open question. In addition, the authors further demonstrate an exit effect of permeation by changing the membrane surfaces that are in contact with either metal catalysts and/or atmosphere gases. Interestingly, these changes seem can remotely influence the permeation process that are separated by defect-free 2D materials.
Personally, I think those phenomenon are interestingly enough for publication at this stage. Nevertheless, I still recommend the authors to exclude the possibility of proton permeation through the interlayer spacing. What is the explanation of the faster permeation of D2 in Fig. S5?
Did the author try gas permeation using hBN bubbles? And what is the activation energy. Important information can be obtained by such experiment.
How the metal nanoparticles being deposited onto the graphene surface? Could they introduce any defects? The metal nanoparticles also seem unevenly distributed all over the surface, say in Fig. S7. Do they appear to be on the bubbles?
Minor suggestions:
1. It is important to add the methods of controlling the number of bubble wall layers, as well as for identifying the number of layers.
2. Page 3, Fig. 1d: the scale of the x-axis (from 25 to 400) appears to be incorrect.
3. Page 5, Fig. 2a: the structural model of the first MoS2 layer appears to be discontinuous (with broken bonds?).
4. Page 15: undefined variables in the equations.
5. Spelling typos, such as '… analyze the date (data?)' in the author's contribution.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript presents a study on hydrogen permeation through defect-free 2D materials, with a focus on graphene. The authors provide experimental evidence that hydrogen can permeate pristine graphene at elevated temperatures in the form of protons. The work is systematic, well-supported by multiple characterization techniques, and offers valuable insights into the catalytic dissociation-permeation mechanism. However, several issues require clarification and additional evidence before the manuscript can be considered for publication.
1. The authors claim their work "overturns the conventional wisdom about the gas permeation barrier for graphene." However, this conventional wisdom was already challenged by Sun et al., Nature 579, 229–232 (2020) (Ref 13), which first reported room-temperature H₂ permeation through defect-free graphene. The current manuscript should differentiate its contributions from this foundational study.
2. The systematic investigation of high-temperature regimes, layer-number independence of E_A, and the role of metal NPs/atmosphere, which significantly expands upon the initial discovery. The introduction and discussion sections should be revised to frame the work as a mechanistic deepening and generalization of the phenomenon first reported by Sun et al., rather than a standalone discovery.
3. While the three-step mechanism is clearly proposed, direct evidence for the catalytic dissociation of H₂ into protons on pristine graphene remains indirect. If would be better if the authors provide more direct spectroscopic or simulation evidence to support this first step.
4. The mechanism by which Pt and Pd NPs reduce the energy barrier is attributed to steps 2&3, but direct evidence is lacking.
5. The finding that E_A is independent of layer number is intriguing but counterintuitive. The authors should discuss possible physical or chemical reasons for this behavior more thoroughly, perhaps with support from theoretical calculations or modeling.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The paper by Xu, et al. reports experimental measurements on a potential scenario of graphene helps with hydrogen dissociation into protons. The topic is interesting which has been proposed and tested both experimentally and theoretically in recent years. However, the referee cannot see the main conclusions claimed in the present manuscript being well supported by experimental results. The referee would not recommend publication due to the following comments:
The authors did not provide necessary experimental details in terms of how to introduce hydrogen into the bubbles. The surfaces are contamination-free is also scientifically wrong, since all surfaces exposing or being prepared in air contains hydrocarbon, which may lead to the fact that gases in the bubble are not pure hydrogen but certain hydrocarbons. See many papers reporting the mechanical properties of bubbles and characterizations using HRTEM for the hydrocarbon adhered on 2D materials’ surfaces.
Following this comment, no experimental proof for the trapped gases being hydrogen was provided, which is required or the whole study would be built on a wrong or improper assumption.
Fig. 1c shows indeed gradual shrinkage of the bubble but this only occurred at higher than 700C, whereas below this threshold temperature, nothing happened. That, is, the claim ‘their volumes progressively decreases’ is misleading. The constant h/R again is suspicious of sort of thermal induced mechanical evolution of 2D bubbles rather than permeation. Or otherwise, h/R would evolve, say at least h would changes while keeping R more or less constant.
‘No interlayer H2 migrations are observed’: Did the authors check the areal density of bubbles before and after annealing to different T? Please provide.
It could be quite surprising to find hydrogen or protons transport across graphene thicker than monolayer and MoS2 of any thicknesses, which contradicts the previous reports. Authors are suggested to provide detailed explanation.
The authors compared PMMA and PEM. The referee here has two comments. On one hand, PMMA could be highly permeable to protons especially in liquids, unless being cross-linked under exposure to high-dose electrons. On the other, these comparisons are so weak that cannot (I am afraid) lead to the conclusion that it was protons that permeate 2D layers. Still no direct evidence is provided.
Previous theory on graphene including those on carbon nanotubes suggested that it was convex rather than concave curvatures that enhanced hydrogen dissociation whereas the concave curvatures facilitated desorption. Additionally, a strong tensile strength (the bubble was always tensed with constant h/R) did not help with hydrogen dissociation into ‘protons’. These theoretical suggestions contradicts the authors’ setup and results, which should be clarified.
The same activation energy for different layers already provided a strong indication that the reduced volume of bubbles was not due to hydrogen/proton permeating 2D layers but due to other possibilities such as interlayer spacing leakage or creation of gas-leak defects. For spacing leakage, authors should check the areal density of bubbles before and after rather than simply claim neighboring bubbles were not affected. The creation of defects could partly reconcile the conflict results of H2/proton permeate MoS2 by the authors and others. Furthermore, although the authors claim no D peak was observed for tested graphene samples in Raman (S8), 1) Raman cannot sense defect density of lower than say 10%; 2) G’ and 2D’ peaks emerge highly indicative of defects.
On the other hand, because the authors found prefactor scales as a function of exp(-N), a more plausible explanation would be the tested species transported layer by layer (for MoS2, the transport would be through high-T induced defects-MoS2 has high-density S vacancies on the surface and also, high catalytic activity). This suggests the tested bubbles that were seemingly sealed by 2L graphene (for example) were essentially composed of bubbles on bubbles and separated by each 1L of graphene. This scenario would reconcile in part the conflict results of H2/proton permeate 2L or thicker graphene by the authors and others.
Whatever cases are, the authors should provide more experimental evidence and explanation, which are rather weak or lack in the present form.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
Report
The manuscript by Jie Xu et al. regards the permeability of two-dimensional crystals to hydrogen. In their manuscript, the authors show that hydrogen permeability is a catalysis-driven process leading to the dissociation of molecular hydrogen at the crystal surface. The topic is relevant for fundamental and practical aspects related to the physics and chemistry of atomically thin gas membranes.
The experiments performed are numerous, generally well conducted and interesting and the set of data reported and related analysis are potentially valuable. The literature quoted is appropriate and complete. Therefore, this manuscript would deserve publication in Nature Communications.
Yet, the manuscript needs important changes. The English requires some corrections. In some instances, the description of the results is not organised in a clear manner, e.g., different materials are considered in diverse experiments that may create confusion. The optical data require a more accurate discussion. The figures are sometimes not explicative and the last part of the work should be rewritten or reorganised. Indeed, the role of the external gas atmosphere in the molecular hydrogen dissociation is a most relevant aspect that requires a clearer presentation and a more detailed discussion of the data.
Specific comments follow.
Abstract. The last lines of the abstract claim that the results reported “establish graphene a catalytic membrane for hydrogen-based technologies, including fuel cells and high-purity hydrogen extraction”. However, this claim is not further demonstrated nor discussed in the manuscript. The conclusions of the present work should somehow address this technological aspect in a more explicit manner. In addition, similar findings are found in MoSe2, MoS2 and h-BN. Why only graphene is given relevance in the title and abstract?
Page 2, line 19. Honestly, I don’t quite understand point (2): What else can be the dissociation species of H2 if not protons?
Page 3, lines 3-5. The process employed to let H2 bubbles form beneath the sample surface would need more details instead of relegating it to few lines in the Methods section. Indeed, the method used by the authors is distinctively different from that employed to create domes in transition metal dichalcogenides and h-BN by a Kaufmann source (refs 24-29) and is instead similar to that used for creating bubbles in h-BN (ref. 30). In particular, the authors should make it clear whether protons or ionised H2 molecules penetrate through the first top layers. I know that this is referenced to previous work by the authors, but given the pivotal role of this process a more explicit mention should be made in the main text.
Page 4, line 4. Why h/R ~ 0.125 indicates that H2 permeate all the dome layers of graphene? What does this sentence mean? I’m not saying that it is wrong, simply I cannot understand it (and likely the readers as well).
Page 4, lines 7 and 8. The Raman data should be discussed more explicitly. Why the presence/absence of D peak is relevant? Personally, I know why. However, another reader may not. Please, provide at least a reference and/or say in the extended data what each Raman peak corresponds to. The authors state that “no interlayer H2 migrations are observed. There are no obvious damage or wrinkles observed on the regions where the H2 bubble disappears by AFM”. While I agree on this statement, yet this aspect would require some more discussion or AFM images taken/shown on a smaller scale length to really make the reader appreciate the absence of damages or wrinkles. This is a crucial aspect of the present work and it deserves more attention.
Extended data Fig. 1. The figure is nice and shows important results, but it is quite confusing: for three different samples, three different sets of data are shown.
2L graphene: optical and AFM images after 900 °C annealing and Raman vs annealing temperature
3L graphene: optical and AFM images before annealing and Raman vs annealing temperature
2L h-BN: AFM images before and after annealing and AFM profile analysis.
This makes the readers’ (and referees’) life hard. If the authors wish, they can leave this figure as it is, but I’d encourage them to make an extra effort to render the figure more rational, if possible.
Extended data Fig. 2. The Raman and photoluminescence (PL) data should be described properly. What are the different Raman peaks (say which Raman peaks are due to the strained bubbles and which ones are due to the bulk material beneath)? Likewise, the PL data are shown without any comment. Are the PL data affected by strain? If the authors feel they cannot explain the PL data, it’d be better to remove them.
Page 4, lines 13-15. The deuterium treatment was performed after the creation of H2 bubbles. Is it quite puzzling that D+ ionises H2 and form HD. Could it be the case that H contamination was present in the D bottle? In addition, the authors should specify that deuterium treatment was performed on h-BN. Was deuterium treatment performed on h-BN, only? This is just a curiosity, I don’t mean that the authors should perform deuterium treatments on the other materials.
Page 5, line 15. Frankly, I’d not say that the power is very weak: 1 mW should result in a power density of about 100 kW/cm2. As a matter of fact, this quite high power density is fully consistent with the observation that temperatures in excess of 700 °C are necessary to observe H2 dissociation.
The experiment described in Fig. 2 and related text is elegant and insightful. I have some questions. Why MoS2 was chosen? Were similar findings observed for graphite and h-BN, too? This point gives me the opportunity to move a general criticism to this work. Often, the authors move from one material to another that creates some confusion and might leave some room for doubts about the general validity of the reported observations.
Referring to Figure 2d, I do not understand the profile shown. It looks like the bubble is 10 nm tall. Are the authors sure that they are not measuring just the PMMA material and no bubble is left beneath? The same apply to extended data Figure 4. My impression that no H2 gas is present any more due to the bubble explosion. Can the authors elucidate this point?
Page 5, line 22. Please, specify the PMMA/PEM thickness.
Page 14. Regarding the calculation of the permeation rate. Is this an ensemble measurement? What the summation index indicates? A summation over different bubbles?
Page 7, lines 27 and 28. There should be a mistake in exp(-N), since this formula seemingly makes no sense.
Figure 4b. I’d suggest to include the NP-free data, too, so that a clear comparison can be done.
The experiment with metallic NPs is very interesting. Have the authors ever considered to use NPs before H treatment? Could the formation of H2 bubbles be promoted by the presence on metal NPs?
Page 9, lines 4-6. The authors state that “it is still puzzled that Pt shows no significant reduction for 3L graphene, which may result from the aggregation and deactivation of Pt NPs at higher temperatures”. Frankly, I find this observation quite sensible and not puzzling at all. Indeed, if the metal NPs are further from the gas-bubble interface, there should be a reduced H2 dissociation. On the contrary, I find it puzzling the absence of a clear reduction of EA with increasing crystal thickness in MoS2.
The experiments involving a different external atmosphere are very intriguing. However, I urge the authors to reformulate this part (from line 15 to line 30 at page 9 and from line 1 to line 2 at page 10) of the manuscript. Both text and Figure 4d are very confusing and hard to follow. The caption of Figure 4d is unacceptable: there is no account and explanation whatsoever of the data and lines shown. I’d prepare a new figure 5 (possibly including the data shown in extended data Fig. 8 and 9; the authors can best decide on this point) entirely devoted to this nice experiment and describe the results in a plain and clear manner by specifying what all lines in the figure are. In particular, a clear comparison between the data obtained in standard annealing experiments (namely, no O2) and in annealing experiments under O2 presence should be made. Similarly, extended data Fig. 8 and 9 are a bit confusing, since the figures compare images taken after annealing at different temperatures and different gas atmospheres. I know that the bubble deflation occurs at different temperature values, but the authors should try to compare images as close as possible in terms of annealing temperatures and experimental conditions. This is particularly true for h-BN in extended data Fig. 9.
Finally, a critical discussion of the implications of the experiments with regards to applicative prospects for catalysis and fuel cell is lacking, despite this aspect was mentioned in the abstract. The authors should discuss this point, also briefly.
In summary, the manuscript sometimes lacks of clarity. The data presentation and related figures are confusing in some instance. Nevertheless, the topic is of high current interest and the results obtained are accurate, relevant and worth being published in Nat. Commun.

## Abstract

Two-dimensional (2D) crystals with atomic-level thickness dramatically shortens the
gas transport pathways, rendering it exceptionally promising for separation membrane
applications. While defect-free 2D crystals such as graphene have long been considered
impermeable to all gases, recent studies show that pristine monolayer graphene permits
room-temperature hydrogen permeation. However, the identity of the permeating species
and its generalizability to other 2D materials remain unclear. Herein, we report hydrogen
permeation behaviour through varying 2D crystals at elevated temperature, and the
hydrogen permeability of graphene can reach up to 1017 s-1m-2 as the form of protons.
This process is evidenced by three critical steps: 2D crystals-assisted catalytic
dissociation of hydrogen into protons, protons permeation through the 2D crystals lattice,
and proton recombination after permeation. Interestingly, the activation energy remains
invariant with the layer number of 2D crystals, but the permeability and activation energy
can be modulated by the type of materials, adsorbed metal nanoparticles, and the
external atmosphere. These findings reveal a catalysis-driven proton permeation
mechanism, and fundamentally deepen the understanding of hydrogen permeation

## Introduction

stability and lifespan of graphene1.

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, the authors demonstrate an intriguing behavior of hydrogen gas permeation through defect-free atomically-thin membranes. Although the report is more phenomenologically, I believe there is fundamentally important mechanisms underneath. Therefore, I highly recommend its publication to the community that may attract more attentions and promote the discovery of new physics.
To my knowledge, catalytic dissociation of hydrogen gas via 2D surfaces at relatively high temperatures (here, up to 900 °C) was not reported previously. More importantly, at this temperature, whether and how proton permeates through multilayer 2D materials remain an interesting open question. In addition, the authors further demonstrate an exit effect of permeation by changing the membrane surfaces that are in contact with either metal catalysts and/or atmosphere gases. Interestingly, these changes seem can remotely influence the permeation process that are separated by defect-free 2D materials.
Personally, I think those phenomenon are interestingly enough for publication at this stage. Nevertheless, I still recommend the authors to exclude the possibility of proton permeation through the interlayer spacing. What is the explanation of the faster permeation of D2 in Fig. S5?
Did the author try gas permeation using hBN bubbles? And what is the activation energy. Important information can be obtained by such experiment.
How the metal nanoparticles being deposited onto the graphene surface? Could they introduce any defects? The metal nanoparticles also seem unevenly distributed all over the surface, say in Fig. S7. Do they appear to be on the bubbles?
Minor suggestions:
1. It is important to add the methods of controlling the number of bubble wall layers, as well as for identifying the number of layers.
2. Page 3, Fig. 1d: the scale of the x-axis (from 25 to 400) appears to be incorrect.
3. Page 5, Fig. 2a: the structural model of the first MoS2 layer appears to be discontinuous (with broken bonds?).
4. Page 15: undefined variables in the equations.
5. Spelling typos, such as '… analyze the date (data?)' in the author's contribution.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a study on hydrogen permeation through defect-free 2D materials, with a focus on graphene. The authors provide experimental evidence that hydrogen can permeate pristine graphene at elevated temperatures in the form of protons. The work is systematic, well-supported by multiple characterization techniques, and offers valuable insights into the catalytic dissociation-permeation mechanism. However, several issues require clarification and additional evidence before the manuscript can be considered for publication.
1. The authors claim their work "overturns the conventional wisdom about the gas permeation barrier for graphene." However, this conventional wisdom was already challenged by Sun et al., Nature 579, 229–232 (2020) (Ref 13), which first reported room-temperature H₂ permeation through defect-free graphene. The current manuscript should differentiate its contributions from this foundational study.
2. The systematic investigation of high-temperature regimes, layer-number independence of E_A, and the role of metal NPs/atmosphere, which significantly expands upon the initial discovery. The introduction and discussion sections should be revised to frame the work as a mechanistic deepening and generalization of the phenomenon first reported by Sun et al., rather than a standalone discovery.
3. While the three-step mechanism is clearly proposed, direct evidence for the catalytic dissociation of H₂ into protons on pristine graphene remains indirect. If would be better if the authors provide more direct spectroscopic or simulation evidence to support this first step.
4. The mechanism by which Pt and Pd NPs reduce the energy barrier is attributed to steps 2&3, but direct evidence is lacking.
5. The finding that E_A is independent of layer number is intriguing but counterintuitive. The authors should discuss possible physical or chemical reasons for this behavior more thoroughly, perhaps with support from theoretical calculations or modeling.

### Reviewer 3

The paper by Xu, et al. reports experimental measurements on a potential scenario of graphene helps with hydrogen dissociation into protons. The topic is interesting which has been proposed and tested both experimentally and theoretically in recent years. However, the referee cannot see the main conclusions claimed in the present manuscript being well supported by experimental results. The referee would not recommend publication due to the following comments:
The authors did not provide necessary experimental details in terms of how to introduce hydrogen into the bubbles. The surfaces are contamination-free is also scientifically wrong, since all surfaces exposing or being prepared in air contains hydrocarbon, which may lead to the fact that gases in the bubble are not pure hydrogen but certain hydrocarbons. See many papers reporting the mechanical properties of bubbles and characterizations using HRTEM for the hydrocarbon adhered on 2D materials’ surfaces.
Following this comment, no experimental proof for the trapped gases being hydrogen was provided, which is required or the whole study would be built on a wrong or improper assumption.
Fig. 1c shows indeed gradual shrinkage of the bubble but this only occurred at higher than 700C, whereas below this threshold temperature, nothing happened. That, is, the claim ‘their volumes progressively decreases’ is misleading. The constant h/R again is suspicious of sort of thermal induced mechanical evolution of 2D bubbles rather than permeation. Or otherwise, h/R would evolve, say at least h would changes while keeping R more or less constant.
‘No interlayer H2 migrations are observed’: Did the authors check the areal density of bubbles before and after annealing to different T? Please provide.
It could be quite surprising to find hydrogen or protons transport across graphene thicker than monolayer and MoS2 of any thicknesses, which contradicts the previous reports. Authors are suggested to provide detailed explanation.
The authors compared PMMA and PEM. The referee here has two comments. On one hand, PMMA could be highly permeable to protons especially in liquids, unless being cross-linked under exposure to high-dose electrons. On the other, these comparisons are so weak that cannot (I am afraid) lead to the conclusion that it was protons that permeate 2D layers. Still no direct evidence is provided.
Previous theory on graphene including those on carbon nanotubes suggested that it was convex rather than concave curvatures that enhanced hydrogen dissociation whereas the concave curvatures facilitated desorption. Additionally, a strong tensile strength (the bubble was always tensed with constant h/R) did not help with hydrogen dissociation into ‘protons’. These theoretical suggestions contradicts the authors’ setup and results, which should be clarified.
The same activation energy for different layers already provided a strong indication that the reduced volume of bubbles was not due to hydrogen/proton permeating 2D layers but due to other possibilities such as interlayer spacing leakage or creation of gas-leak defects. For spacing leakage, authors should check the areal density of bubbles before and after rather than simply claim neighboring bubbles were not affected. The creation of defects could partly reconcile the conflict results of H2/proton permeate MoS2 by the authors and others. Furthermore, although the authors claim no D peak was observed for tested graphene samples in Raman (S8), 1) Raman cannot sense defect density of lower than say 10%; 2) G’ and 2D’ peaks emerge highly indicative of defects.
On the other hand, because the authors found prefactor scales as a function of exp(-N), a more plausible explanation would be the tested species transported layer by layer (for MoS2, the transport would be through high-T induced defects-MoS2 has high-density S vacancies on the surface and also, high catalytic activity). This suggests the tested bubbles that were seemingly sealed by 2L graphene (for example) were essentially composed of bubbles on bubbles and separated by each 1L of graphene. This scenario would reconcile in part the conflict results of H2/proton permeate 2L or thicker graphene by the authors and others.
Whatever cases are, the authors should provide more experimental evidence and explanation, which are rather weak or lack in the present form.

### Reviewer 4

Report
The manuscript by Jie Xu et al. regards the permeability of two-dimensional crystals to hydrogen. In their manuscript, the authors show that hydrogen permeability is a catalysis-driven process leading to the dissociation of molecular hydrogen at the crystal surface. The topic is relevant for fundamental and practical aspects related to the physics and chemistry of atomically thin gas membranes.
The experiments performed are numerous, generally well conducted and interesting and the set of data reported and related analysis are potentially valuable. The literature quoted is appropriate and complete. Therefore, this manuscript would deserve publication in Nature Communications.
Yet, the manuscript needs important changes. The English requires some corrections. In some instances, the description of the results is not organised in a clear manner, e.g., different materials are considered in diverse experiments that may create confusion. The optical data require a more accurate discussion. The figures are sometimes not explicative and the last part of the work should be rewritten or reorganised. Indeed, the role of the external gas atmosphere in the molecular hydrogen dissociation is a most relevant aspect that requires a clearer presentation and a more detailed discussion of the data.
Specific comments follow.
Abstract. The last lines of the abstract claim that the results reported “establish graphene a catalytic membrane for hydrogen-based technologies, including fuel cells and high-purity hydrogen extraction”. However, this claim is not further demonstrated nor discussed in the manuscript. The conclusions of the present work should somehow address this technological aspect in a more explicit manner. In addition, similar findings are found in MoSe2, MoS2 and h-BN. Why only graphene is given relevance in the title and abstract?
Page 2, line 19. Honestly, I don’t quite understand point (2): What else can be the dissociation species of H2 if not protons?
